summary: Log analysis of 291 Japanese junior-high students answering 29,963 EFL grammar-drill questions built from ~55,000 GPT-4.1-mini-generated English-Japanese sentences tagged to CEFR-J grammar levels. Reports descriptive accuracy/latency by question type (MCQ easiest, cloze hardest to self-correct, drag-and-drop slowest) and by CEFR level (accuracy falls from 79.13% at A1.1 to 50.88% at B2.2).

claims.claim: Question modality creates a performance hierarchy: MCQ 76.9% first-try, drag-and-drop 74.5%, cloze 69.2%; drag-and-drop slowest (median >7.5s).
claims.evidence: §4 RQ1, Figures 3-4; descriptive only, no significance tests or mixed-effects model despite repeated measures per student.

claims.claim: Learner data validate the CEFR-J grammar hierarchy (accuracy declines, latency rises with level).
claims.evidence: §4 RQ2, Figures 5-6; non-monotonic anomalies (MCQ A2.2 63.06% < B1.1 67.02%; latency falls at B2); self-selection into levels confounds difficulty (acknowledged §5.3); B2.2 has only 256 attempts.

claims.claim: LLMs can successfully generate learning content.
claims.evidence: No audit of generated sentences for grammaticality, translation accuracy, or level fit, and no comparison with teacher-written items; both are listed as future work (§5.3 'Content Validation'). Student accuracy trends do not measure content quality.

methodology.sample: 291 students from one high-performing Japanese junior high school; 29,963 attempts after removing timeouts, top-5% latency tail and 5,662 rapid-guess MCQs (<1.04s KDE cutoff).
methodology.baselines: None (no teacher-written or non-LLM content comparison).
methodology.variance: None; descriptive percentages and medians only.

standards.artifacts: No data, prompts, or app code released.
standards.preregistration: None mentioned for a human-subjects log study.

biases.detail: Single high-performing school; students self-select CEFR level filters (acknowledged).
Student accuracy is used as evidence that LLM-generated content is valid, without assessing the content itself.
No CIs, tests, or per-student modelling.
Generated corpus and prompts not released.

coi.affiliations: Kyoto University and Ritsumeikan University; authors appear to operate the Grammar Gretel app studied.
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Authors' own educational app; GPT-4.1-mini used as a generator, not evaluated.
coi.detail: Authors evaluate their own app's content with their own logs, but no commercial interest stated.

verdict_reason: off-topic: EFL grammar-drill learner analytics, not LLM agents or software engineering. Its headline claim that LLM-generated content is pedagogically viable is never tested (no content audit, no teacher-written comparison) and the analysis is descriptive only.
applicability: Does not inform any harness decision. The only tangential lesson for a healthcare-education content team is negative: learner performance logs are not a substitute for validating LLM-generated content; ingestion pipelines that accept LLM-generated items should carry explicit content QA (expert review or automated levelers/validators) before delivery to front ends. No relevance to Java, multi-repo ingestion, mixed agent hosts, or spec-driven development.
